title: Chapter XVIII

teacherSummary.text: Back in Geneva, Victor delays. His father asks whether he loves another; Victor agrees to marry Elizabeth after a trip to England, where he will secretly do his work. He travels with Clerval through Germany and down the Rhine.

vocabulary.definition: To pluck up by the roots
vocabulary.context: My father saw this change with pleasure, and he turned his thoughts towards the best method of eradicating the remains of my melancholy, which every now and then would return by fits, and with a devouring blackness overcast the approaching sunshine.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.context: For myself, there was one reward I promised myself from my detested toils—one consolation for my unparalleled sufferings; it was the prospect of that day when, enfranchised from my miserable slavery, I might claim Elizabeth, and forget the past in my union with her.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.context: It had been her care which provided me a companion in Clerval—and yet a man is blind to a thousand minute circumstances, which call forth a woman’s sedulous attention.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: A winding, crooked, or involved course
vocabulary.context: In one spot you view rugged hills, ruined castles overlooking tremendous precipices, with the dark Rhine rushing beneath; and, on the sudden turn of a promontory, flourishing vineyards, with green sloping banks, and a meandering river, and populous towns occupy the scene.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: Inclined to defer or put off what ought to be done at once
vocabulary.context: The latter method of obtaining the desired intelligence was dilatory and unsatisfactory: besides, I had an insurmountable aversion to the idea of engaging myself in my loathsome task in my father’s house, while in habits of familiar intercourse with those I loved.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.context: Oh, surely, the spirit that inhabits and guards this place has a soul more in harmony with man, than those who pile the glacier, or retire to the inaccessible peaks of the mountains of our own country.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: The entrance of an enemy into a country with purposes of hostility
vocabulary.context: My journey had been my own suggestion, and Elizabeth, therefore, acquiesced: but she was filled with disquiet at the idea of my suffering, away from her, the inroads of misery and grief.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: An implement of agriculture, usually formed of pieces of timber or metal crossing each other, and set with iron or…
vocabulary.context: I was aware also that I should often lose all self-command, all capacity of hiding the harrowing sensations that would possess me during the progress of my unearthly occupation.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: Having no example or similar case
vocabulary.context: Pardon this gush of sorrow; these ineffectual words are but a slight tribute to the unexampled worth of Henry, but they soothe my heart, overflowing with the anguish which his remembrance creates.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: Having marks or patches of different colors
vocabulary.context: This part of the Rhine, indeed, presents a singularly variegated landscape.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

context.history: The Rhine was celebrated for picturesque castles and vineyards in Romantic travel writing.

significance: Clerval's joy in nature contrasts with Victor's dread, heightening tension.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XVIII,” how does Shelley show delay and dread? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the foreshadowing you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XVIII develops the idea of delay and dread. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of foreshadowing and setting shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses foreshadowing in Chapter XVIII to complicate the reader's understanding of delay and dread. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XVIII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of delay and dread responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XVIII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of delay and dread. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

satQuestions.passage: To England, therefore, I was bound, and it was understood that my union with Elizabeth should take place immediately on my return. My father’s age rendered him extremely averse to delay. For myself, there was one reward I promised myself from my detested toils—one consolation for my unparalleled sufferings; it was the prospect of that day when, enfranchised from my miserable slavery, I might claim Elizabeth, and forget the past in my union with her.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter XVIII”?

segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: How does Clerval's attitude toward nature differ from Victor's at this point? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include eradicating, enfranchised, sedulous, meandering, dilatory. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: “My father saw this change with pleasure, and he turned his thoughts towards the best method of eradicating the remains of my melancholy, which every now and then would return by fits, and with a devouring blackness overcast the approaching sunshine.” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: To pluck up by the roots.

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. The Rhine was celebrated for picturesque castles and vineyards in Romantic travel writing. Now, why does this chapter matter? Clerval's joy in nature contrasts with Victor's dread, heightening tension. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Foreshadowing, Setting, Characterization.
segments.script: Let's read this passage together. I will read the first sentence; you track along. Every time you spot foreshadowing, mark it. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice here? I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.
segments.passage: To England, therefore, I was bound, and it was understood that my union with Elizabeth should take place immediately on my return. My father’s age rendered him extremely averse to delay. For myself, there was one reward I promised myself from my detested toils—one consolation for my unparalleled sufferings; it was the prospect of that day when, enfranchised from my miserable slavery, I might claim Elizabeth, and forget the past in my union with her.
